name: Shag Harbour
summary: El 4 de octubre de 1967, varios residentes de Shag Harbour (Nueva Escocia) vieron un objeto con cuatro luces caer al mar; la RCMP confirmó en minutos la espuma amarilla y una mancha persistente. El Maritime Command ordenó una búsqueda submarina de tres días de la Fleet Diving Unit, y el gobierno liberó los registros sin disputa.
summary_en: On 4 October 1967, several Shag Harbour (Nova Scotia) residents saw a four-light object fall into the sea; the RCMP confirmed yellow foam and a lingering slick within minutes. Maritime Command ordered a three-day underwater search by the Fleet Diving Unit, and the government released the records without dispute.

evidenceContribution.rationale: Royal Canadian Navy + Royal Canadian Mounted Police investigaron crash de objeto en aguas de Shag Harbour (Nova Scotia) el 4 octubre 1967. Multi-witness institucional (RCMP officers + civilian pilots + 11+ residents + Coast Guard) observaron objeto descender al agua con luces orange/yellow flashing. Buque HMCS Granby ejecutó dive search formal por dos días buscando wreckage. Caso es uno de los pocos UAP officially registrados como 'unsolved' por la Canadian government en archivos desclasificados. Substantial weakens porque Navy investigation + multi-witness + physical search + dive operation es modalidad evidencial robusta que excluye fenómeno atmosférico.
evidenceContribution.rationaleEn: Royal Canadian Navy + Royal Canadian Mounted Police investigated the crash of an object into Shag Harbour waters (Nova Scotia) on October 4, 1967. Institutional multi-witness (RCMP officers + civilian pilots + 11+ residents + Coast Guard) observed the object descend into the water with flashing orange/yellow lights. HMCS Granby executed a formal two-day dive search for wreckage. Case is one of the few UAP officially registered as 'unsolved' by the Canadian government in declassified files. Substantial weakens because Navy investigation + multi-witness + physical search + dive operation is a robust evidential modality that excludes atmospheric phenomenon.

evidenceContribution.rationale: Comportamiento transmedium aire-agua + sustained underwater activity reportada por divers en operación HMCS Granby + objeto no recuperado a pesar de búsqueda formal implica craft con capacidad submarina sustained no compatible con tecnología naval canadiense/aliada 1967. Modest sin observación de entidad directa.
evidenceContribution.rationaleEn: Transmedium air-water behavior + sustained underwater activity reported by divers in HMCS Granby operation + object not recovered despite formal search implies craft with sustained underwater capability not compatible with 1967 Canadian/allied naval technology. Modest without direct entity observation.

whatHappened:
El 4 de octubre de 1967 a las 23:20 hora local, múltiples residentes de Shag Harbour (Nueva Escocia, Canadá) y pueblos cercanos reportaron ver un objeto con cuatro luces brillantes descender en ángulo y caer al agua a aproximadamente 800 metros de la costa. Reportaron una explosión audible y observaron espuma amarilla flotando sobre el lugar del impacto.

La Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) respondió en minutos. Tres oficiales en una lancha confirmaron la espuma amarilla y una mancha persistente de aproximadamente 800m × 30m. La RCMP transmitió telexes de prioridad al Maritime Command (RCN) y al Air Defence Command (RCAF). El Maritime Command despachó la Fleet Diving Unit Atlantic — una unidad de buzos militares — que realizó una búsqueda submarina exhaustiva durante tres días. La búsqueda fue documentada en registros oficiales del Department of National Defence (DND).

Los resultados de la búsqueda fueron clasificados inicialmente. En documentos liberados décadas después, el DND canadiense reportó: 'No se encontró nada que pudiera identificarse como origen de la observación inicial.' El caso permanece como el único 'crash' UAP donde la respuesta multi-agencia militar gubernamental fue documentada contemporáneamente y los registros oficiales han sido liberados sin disputa por el Gobierno de Canadá.
whatHappened_en:
On October 4, 1967 at 23:20 local time, multiple residents of Shag Harbour (Nova Scotia, Canada) and nearby towns reported seeing an object with four bright lights descend at an angle and crash into the water approximately 800 meters offshore. They reported an audible explosion and observed yellow foam floating on the impact site.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) responded within minutes. Three officers in a launch confirmed the yellow foam and a persistent slick of approximately 800m × 30m. The RCMP transmitted priority telexes to Maritime Command (RCN) and Air Defence Command (RCAF). Maritime Command dispatched the Fleet Diving Unit Atlantic — a military divers unit — which conducted an exhaustive undersea search over three days. The search was documented in official Department of National Defence (DND) records.

The search results were initially classified. In documents released decades later, Canadian DND reported: 'Nothing was found that could be identified as the origin of the initial observation.' The case remains the only UAP 'crash' where the multi-agency military government response was contemporaneously documented and the official records have been released without dispute by the Government of Canada.
whyMatters: Único caso UAP de 'crash' donde la respuesta gubernamental multi-agencia es documentada contemporáneamente y los registros oficiales han sido liberados sin disputa por el gobierno (a diferencia de Roswell o Kecksburg). La búsqueda submarina del Fleet Diving Unit Atlantic durante 3 días bajo orden del Maritime Command transforma esto de testimonio civil a operación militar registrada. Establece precedente de transparencia institucional en investigación UAP.
whyMatters_en: The only UAP 'crash' case where the multi-agency government response is contemporaneously documented and the official records have been released without dispute by the government (unlike Roswell or Kecksburg). The Fleet Diving Unit Atlantic's 3-day undersea search under Maritime Command order transforms this from civilian testimony to a recorded military operation. Establishes precedent of institutional transparency in UAP investigation.
